Master thesis · May 2026

Machine-learning detection of motion artefacts in diaphragmatic EMG

Surface EMG over the diaphragm shows breathing effort directly, which makes it a strong candidate for wearable respiratory monitoring. Body movement corrupts the signal. I built a framework that finds the motion-contaminated parts automatically, from the EMG signal alone.

Supervised by Prof. Sadasivan Puthusserypady (DTU Health Tech), with Søren Straarup Rasmussen and Jacopo Mattia de A. Constantini.

95.4%accuracy on unseen subjects
86%Motion F1-score
15volunteers recorded, plus 3 external
23time, statistical and spectral features
STEP 1 · DATA COLLECTION

A recording protocol built around movement

Two electrodes and a reference over the lower ribs. Each volunteer went through 16 short blocks, mostly one minute each: rest in different postures, turning, leg flexion, torso rotation, chair steps and abdominal crunches. Spirometry was recorded alongside.

STEP 2 · ECG REMOVAL & LABELLING

Clean the heart out, then mark the movement

The heart's electrical activity dominates chest EMG, so a U-Net decomposition removes the ECG first. I then wrote a GUI to annotate every motion interval by hand, which gave the ground truth for training.

STEP 3 · FEATURES

Sliding windows become feature vectors

The signal is cut into overlapping windows. A window counts as motion when enough of it overlaps an annotated interval. Each window becomes a 23-dimensional vector: amplitude measures like RMS and MAV, statistics like kurtosis, and spectral band powers.

STEP 4 · HONEST EVALUATION

Split by person, choose by more than accuracy

Subjects were split, not windows: 12 for 5-fold cross-validation and 3 held out until the end, so no person appears in both training and testing. A multi-criteria decision analysis then weighed accuracy, speed and simplicity across the classifiers. A Coarse Tree came out on top.

STEP 5 · TUNING

10,192 models trained on the DTU HPC cluster

I ran a full grid search over 57 window lengths × 14 step sizes × 13 overlap thresholds. Each of the 10,192 combinations was a complete train-and-test run, distributed as parallel MATLAB batch jobs on DTU's HPC cluster. Segmentation turned out to matter as much as the classifier. Accuracy peaks around a 4 s window. The final setting was a 4 s window, 0.9 s step and an overlap threshold of about 0.7.

STEP 6 · RESULT

It works on people it has never seen

On external recordings with intentional movement and heavy breathing, the model marks the motion periods and leaves calm breathing alone. The model is easy to read: Mean Absolute Value alone carries about 72% of the decision.

Reliable artefact detection does not need a heavy model. A shallow tree on well-chosen EMG features is fast enough to run on a wearable.

Current · AUSCORA

Lung-sound analysis for a COPD wearable

At AUSCORA I work on the signal-processing and machine-learning side of a chest-worn acoustic sensor for people with COPD. The aim is to follow each breath and find the abnormal sounds that point to a flare-up. I have worked through the pipeline one stage at a time.

  1. STAGE 1

    Heart-sound removal

    A 1D U-Net trained on synthetic mixtures of breathing and real heart recordings separates heart sounds from lung sounds near the heart.

  2. STAGE 2

    Breathing-cycle detection

    Frame-level loudness and slope features feed a tree-ensemble classifier. Rhythm-aware post-processing then turns the scores into individual breaths. I compared 14 model types and evaluated each one on patients held out from training.

  3. NEXT

    Crackles and wheezes

    Classifying adventitious sounds breath by breath, and validating on the device's own recordings.
